passage:
Monday. In the class chat Tejas wrote, "Yes, you can post my dance photo in the fest album, Hrithik." Hrithik did.
Thursday. Tejas opened his phone and saw the same photo in a big group of strangers, with a joke caption. His face went warm. He messaged Hrithik: "I said yes to the fest album, not this. Please take it down." For an hour there was no reply, and Tejas felt his chest tighten.
Saturday. Hrithik wrote, "Deleted it. I thought a yes was a yes for everything. Sorry." Tejas replied, "Ask each time, okay?" Hrithik sent a thumbs-up, and this time he added, "Can I share the fest photo on my page?" Tejas said, "Not today."

qa.q: On which day did Tejas say Hrithik could post the photo?
qa.a: He said so on Monday, in the class chat.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling on Thursday when he saw the photo in the big group?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and anxious, shown by his warm face and tight chest. He might also have felt betrayed, since he had agreed only to the fest album.

qa.q: What should Tejas do if someone pressured or threatened him about sharing more pictures?
qa.a: Not give in, keep the messages, and tell a trusted adult or report it to the school or platform.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have understood the first yes?
qa.a: He may honestly have thought one yes covered any sharing, until Tejas explained that it did not.

grounding: Saying yes once does not authorize everything, and consent to share can be withdrawn.

passage: When I was about your age, Jeevan, and yes, this is your uncle Anirban talking, my friend Ravi asked to see my location on a school trek. I said yes, for that day, and I meant it. Weeks later he kept the sharing on and one evening messaged, "Send me a photo of where you are right now, or I'll tell everyone something about you." My hands went cold. That was no friend. I turned off the sharing, and I did not answer him. I showed the messages to my father, who took them to the school. Saying yes once didn't mean yes forever, and I've told my own kids that. You can always take a yes back, and if anyone frightens you for it, tell someone you trust. Nobody hides that.

qa.q: Where did Anirban's friend ask to see his location?
qa.a: He asked on a school trek.

qa.q: What did Anirban feel when he read Ravi's message?
qa.a: His cold hands suggest he was scared, and he realised the person was not acting as a friend. Anger may also have been mixed in.

qa.q: What did Anirban do that Jeevan could copy?
qa.a: He turned off the sharing, did not reply, kept the messages and showed them to his father, who took them to the school.

qa.q: How might Ravi have seen the situation?
qa.a: He may have thought the earlier yes still counted, but the threat shows he was pressuring Anirban, which is not acceptable. 🤍

grounding: An elder recalls that consent to share location can be withdrawn and that threats should be reported.

passage:
The train to Lonavala was late, the platform was jammed, and Irawati's phone was on nine percent. Before the class trip she had turned on location sharing with Sharmila, just for the day, so they wouldn't lose each other.
Now, three days later, Sharmila's message popped up: "Haha I can see you're at the tuition centre, why aren't you answering?"
Irawati frowned. She had forgotten it was still on.
On the crowded platform, with the battery dropping, she typed: "Hey, I said yes for the trip only. Turning it off now, okay?"
For a second she worried Sharmila would sulk.
The reply came fast: "Oh! Totally, my bad. Your location, your call."
Irawati switched it off with one percent to spare, feeling lighter. She added a note in her phone: sharing = for one thing, not forever.

qa.q: What percent was Irawati's phone battery on the platform?
qa.a: Irawati's phone was on nine percent.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when she saw Sharmila's message three days later?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and a little exposed, because the location sharing she had agreed to for one day was still showing where she was. She also worried Sharmila might sulk.

qa.q: Which choice worked well, and why?
qa.a: Irawati clearly withdrew her yes and Sharmila respected it at once, which kept the friendship easy and her privacy safe.

qa.q: What would change if Sharmila had pushed back or insisted on keeping the sharing on?
qa.a: Then Sharmila's pressure would be a warning sign, and Irawati would need to turn it off anyway and tell a trusted adult.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager learning that consent to share her location for one day can be withdrawn, and a friend respecting it.

passage:
In the Chennai apartment's clubhouse, after the dance show, Rukmini posed with the whole group for Kavitha's phone. "You can post the group one," Rukmini said.
That evening Kavitha messaged: "Also posting the one of you mid-spin, it's hilarious! 😄"
Rukmini opened it. Hair flying, mouth wide open, one eye shut. Her stomach dropped. She typed "no pls," deleted it, and typed it again.
"I said yes to the group photo," she wrote. "Not that one. Please don't."
Kavitha: "It's harmless, everyone will laugh."
Rukmini: "That's the problem. It's my face. No."
Three minutes of nothing. Rukmini sat on her bed, heart thumping.
Then: "Okay, fair. Deleted it from my phone too. Sorry 🙂"
Rukmini breathed out. Next morning she told her mother about it anyway, and her mother said she was proud she'd been clear.

qa.q: Which photo had Rukmini agreed Kavitha could post?
qa.a: Rukmini said Kavitha could post the group one.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling while she waited for Kavitha's reply?
qa.a: She was anxious and tense, sitting with her heart thumping, afraid Kavitha might post the photo anyway or be annoyed.

qa.q: How could a friend like Kavitha handle a request like Rukmini's?
qa.a: Accept the no straight away and delete the photo, as Kavitha finally did, because agreeing to one photo does not cover every picture of a person.

qa.q: How might Kavitha see the mid-spin photo at first compared with Rukmini?
qa.a: Kavitha first saw it as a funny, harmless picture, while for Rukmini it was her own face shown in a way she did not agree to.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager learning that saying yes to one photo does not cover others, and firmly withdrawing consent.

passage:
"Jatin, can I tell you something? Don't laugh."
"I won't. What is it?"
"Remember that gaming guy, the one I thought was our age? I let him see my location once, when he said he'd send a team jersey."
"Okay..."
"I turned it off. Now he keeps messaging. He says if I don't switch it back on, he'll post my photo in the group and say things."
Jatin stopped walking. "Zeenat, that's not okay. He's threatening you."
"I said yes once, though."
"Once doesn't mean forever. You're allowed to take it back. And he's unsafe. We're going to Mrs Pereira right now, before the bell."
They went to the counsellor's room together. Mrs Pereira listened, told Zeenat it was not her fault, and helped her save the messages, block him and report the account. She phoned Zeenat's mother before lunch.

qa.q: What did the gaming contact say he would send Zeenat?
qa.a: He said he'd send a team jersey.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling as she told Jatin about the messages?
qa.a: She was frightened and ashamed, asking him not to laugh and blaming herself because she had said yes once.

qa.q: Which of Jatin's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Jatin named the threat as unsafe, told Zeenat she could withdraw her yes, and took her to the counsellor straight away instead of waiting.

qa.q: How did Mrs Pereira respond, and what would change if she had waited?
qa.a: She listened, said it was not Zeenat's fault, helped save, block and report, and called Zeenat's mother that same morning; waiting would leave Zeenat alone with the threats.

grounding: The dialogue shows a teen learning that one yes to share location can be withdrawn, and that a person who threatens is unsafe and should be reported.

passage: Looking back, the photo wasn't even embarrassing when I sent it. It was me in the lion costume from the school play, mane sliding off, and I sent it to Sumit because he'd missed the show. That was a yes to him seeing it. Last month Sumit messaged: "posting the lion pic on the class page, it's hilarious." I wrote, "please don't, I'm not okay with that." He sent a laughing face, then: "you already sent it, so it's mine now. keep complaining and I'll add your old voice note too." My hands went cold. That same evening I showed Amma the chat. She didn't scold me for sending it. She said, "Saying yes once doesn't mean yes forever, Jeevan beta," and we emailed Mrs Pillai, the class teacher, that night with screenshots. She replied within the hour: she'd speak to Sumit first thing. The photo never went up.

qa.q: What costume was Jeevan wearing in the photo?
qa.a: Jeevan was wearing the lion costume from the school play.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when Sumit's threat arrived?
qa.a: Jeevan felt frightened and trapped, with hands going cold. There may also have been hurt that someone trusted with the photo turned it into a threat.

qa.q: Which steps protected Jeevan?
qa.a: Jeevan said no clearly, showed Amma the chat that same evening, and they emailed Mrs Pillai with screenshots; she replied within the hour and dealt with Sumit next morning.

qa.q: What would change if Amma had scolded Jeevan for sending the photo?
qa.a: Jeevan might have felt ashamed and hidden the next problem, and the threat might not have been reported in time.

grounding: It shows a teenager learning that agreeing to share one photo does not authorise everything, and reporting a peer's pressure and threat to trusted adults.
